newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebel spokesman rejects talks outside house.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebel spokesman rejects talks outside house.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 73 captives in the Japanese ambassador's residence will reject Peruvian government plans for peace talks outside the diplomatic mansion, their international spokesman said on Saturday.
"A meeting has to be within the residence," Isaac Velazco the international spokesman for the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) told Reuters by telephone from Copenhagen.

Government negotiator, Education Minister Domingo Palermo, said on Friday arrangements had been made for talks to solve the month-old crisis with rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini in a building near the besieged compound.
He said the Red Cross and Canada's ambassador would attend the talks as "guarantors."
But Velazco said these observers could not "guarantee the physical safety of the commander."
Although Palermo presented the meeting as definite -- adding that a Red Cross vehicle would transport Cerpa to the site -- it was not clear if the rebels had agreed to it.
"I think the government -- with its speculative statements -- is trying to spoil the negotiation process," Velazco said.
The rebels inside the booby-trapped and mined compound in Lima, ignored on Saturday the opportunity of replying to the government's declared meeting.
Instead they launched a fresh propaganda offensive, unfurling three banners that struck comparisons between their VIP hostages, Peru's poor and their jailed comrades.

"Most of the population would like to feed themselves as well as the authorities held here," read one message, referring to the meals provided daily by the Red Cross during the 32-day siege. "These differences justify the people's struggle."

On two more banners the rebels said the captive officials were "responsible for the government's policies that affect the people" and that the guerrillas' jailed comrades also had families that wanted freedom for their relatives.
Using night-vision lenses, local television showed rebels in the early hours scurrying across the building's roof and hanging down large, white sheets with neat black letters.
About half an hour later, three men came out again to erect their red and white MRTA flag that depicts a mace and rifle flanking the long-haired 18th century Indian revolutionary leader Tupac Amaru.
The publicity stunt showed the two sides were as entrenched in the same uncompromising positions as they had since the siege began on Dec. 17.

Palermo met Cerpa inside the residence on Dec. 28, but two attempts to hold a second round of face-to-face talks have stalled. Last Sunday a planned meeting collapsed because the government refused to discuss the rebels' main demand that some 400 of their jailed comrades be released.
Palermo said on Friday the government was ready to resume talks but would not accept this demand.
Velazco said the MRTA's "global proposal" was negotiable, but that the rebels would not discuss their main demand separately.
The rebels have also called for better prison conditions, a revamping of the judicial system for accused terrorists and a reorganization of the economy to favour the poor.

In Tokyo, Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he believed Peru chose Canada as a talks' observer -- and not Spain or Italy as suggested by the rebels -- to try to prevent the standoff spreading to Europe.
"Probably they want to keep it within the Americas," Hashimoto told reporters.
Since storming the compound, the rebels have released more than 550 of the guests they originally seized at a lavish cocktail party.
On Friday they released their first hostage in 17 days, allowing Luis Valencia Hirano, head of the Delta special forces unit of the anti-terrorist police DINCOTE, to leave for health reasons.

The MRTA has held onto those men it considers the best bargaining chips, including top government and security force officials, dozens of Japanese businessmen and diplomats and the younger brother of President Alberto Fujimori.
Velazco said in part the rebels held the Japanese captive as a deterrent to Fujimori using force to end the siege.
"If they had been freed, Fujimori would by now have tried to occupy the residence militarily," the spokesman said.
